The US Department of Energy (DOE) announced on Nov 3 contract awards for the exchange of 300,000 barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate (fuel oil) from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve (NEHHOR), with fuel supplied from storage sites in Boston, Massachusetts, and New Haven, Connecticut, DOE said. The awards followed DOE's Oct 21, 2026 request for proposals, and fuel transfers or deliveries were scheduled to be completed by Nov 6, 2026. Reuters reported on Nov 4 that the four recipients are Global Companies LLC, Sprague Operating Resources LLC, Trafigura Trading LLC and Vitol Inc., and that the volume is nearly a third of the 1-million-barrel reserve. Under the awarded contracts, recipients will return the same volume of fuel oil plus a premium, so NEHHOR is refilled ahead of the 2027-2028 heating season, DOE said.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced on Oct 29 contract awards for an exchange of more than 40 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), including volumes offered through previous solicitations. The awards are part of DOE's execution of President Trump's 172-million-barrel release, which contributes to a coordinated 400-million-barrel action by International Energy Agency (IEA) member nations' strategic reserves. DOE Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit said the latest awards of more than 40 million barrels complete the US commitment to release 172 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and that DOE has secured the return of more than 216 million barrels to the reserve beginning early next year, including 44 million additional premium barrels, with a value of more than $4 billion, at no additional cost to taxpayers. Crude oil under the awarded contracts will be supplied from the SPR's Big Hill and Bryan Mound storage sites, and DOE will coordinate with awardees, pipelines, terminals and refining partners on the movement of the crude. The award resolves the open 17-million-barrel solicitation issued Oct 16, whose proposals were due Oct 21 and which the status checks on this page had found still unawarded as of the morning of Oct 29; the announcement was published on energy.gov on the afternoon of Oct 29.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 30 that the United States completed the last major portion of its contribution to the broader International Energy Agency release agreement this week: the Energy Department said companies agreed to borrow about 40 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, awarding nearly 16.8 million barrels on Oct 28 after awarding 23.8 million barrels earlier in October. Crude oil gave back ground on Oct 29 as traders weighed the emergency supply against tentative efforts to reopen talks with Iran, OilPrice.com said, with December WTI futures trading at $102.77, down $0.67, at 0005 GMT on Oct 30 and Brent settling Oct 29 at $114.88 a barrel, down $0.44 on the day. The reserve is delivering barrels but remains near its lowest level since 1982, and no agreement has been reached in the renewed diplomatic contact between Washington, Tehran and Qatar, the report said.

The US Department of Energy (DOE) announced on Oct 23, 2026 the authorization of an emergency exchange of up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) to address a crude oil supply disruption affecting the Phillips 66 Lake Charles Refinery in Louisiana, DOE said in a press release on energy.gov. The Energy Department authorized the exchange from the West Hackberry SPR site for immediate delivery. Under the terms of the exchange, all borrowed crude oil will be returned with additional premium barrels, helping replenish and strengthen the SPR at no additional cost to taxpayers, DOE said. DOE Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit said the exchange helps alleviate supply disruption and requires Phillips 66 to return more barrels to the SPR than are currently being withdrawn. A Phillips 66 spokesperson confirmed the refinery will receive crude from the SPR and said the company does not anticipate impacts to Lake Charles operations, Reuters reported on Oct 23. The Lake Charles refinery can process about 264,000 b/d. DOE did not specify what caused the disruption, the final delivery volume, the premium amount, or a repayment deadline in the announcement.

The US Department of Energy said on Oct 21 that it will loan up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve in Maine, Massachusetts and Connecticut, with deliveries set to be completed by Nov 13, Reuters reported. There will be a competitive bidding process for the loans for both fuel retailers and terminal holders. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration was committed to doing everything in its power to lower energy costs. Senator Susan Collins said on X the move equals a 13 percent supply increase for New England and will push down the region's heating oil costs this winter, while Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser at Gulf Oil, said on X the move was puzzling and probably inconsequential and should have no impact on prices. Average retail diesel prices have hovered around $6.32 a gallon in recent days after hitting a record of $6.52 last month, according to AAA. Reuters noted the administration has already agreed to loan 172 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with levels at their lowest since 1982.

The physical shortfall the SPR exchanges are meant to offset deepened last week: intensified attacks on commercial vessels cut Gulf crude flows sharply to about 8.5 million b/d on a seven-day average from more than 20 million b/d the week before, analytics firm Kpler said in a note on Friday cited by Reuters on Oct 19, with at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels reported last week.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposals on Oct 16 for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), Reuters reported. The round is a portion of the pending 40 million barrels that form the last batch of the US 172-million-barrel commitment under the March IEA coordinated release of 400 million barrels. The US has released about 132.5 million barrels from the SPR since the war began. DOE has not published awards from the late September re-offer of the 40 million barrels, but Friday's 17-million-barrel figure implies about 23 million barrels were awarded in that round, Energy Aspects wrote in a note cited by Reuters.

Status check on Oct 16: no DOE award announcement for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange had been published since bids closed Oct 6, and no new SPR exchange or sale authorization had followed the Oct 10 emergency 4-million-barrel Hurricane Isaias exchange. The ledger therefore still stands at up to 44 million barrels committed for November and December delivery, with returns plus premium barrels due from 2027.

Two SPR exchange threads are open at once and are tracked here as one ledger. The first is the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange under the IEA-coordinated release: bids closed October 6 and the award is still pending. The second is an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels authorized October 10 for Hurricane Isaias disruptions. Combined, up to 44 million barrels of reserve crude is committed to move into the Gulf market in November and December 2026, every barrel a loan due back with premium barrels starting in 2027.

DOE issued the request for proposals for the sixth and final 40-million-barrel exchange, drawn from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on October 6 and deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026. Borrowers return the oil plus premium barrels.
The bid window for the 40-million-barrel exchange closed at 11 a.m. CT. As of October 12, DOE has not announced the award; the award announcement is the next dated event on this ledger.

DOE authorized an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels, 2 million each to ExxonMobil and BP America, to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias. The borrowed crude plus premium barrels is to be returned in 2027; ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

Next on the ledger: awarded exchanges under the 40-million-barrel tranche deliver through November and December 2026. Returns begin in 2027, with exchange returns running through 2029; earlier phases returned an average premium of about 25 percent, which DOE says expands long-term reserve inventory at no taxpayer cost.

DOE's per-site grade table as of August 20, 2026 showed 101.8 million barrels of sweet and 192.3 million of sour (294.1 million total), or roughly 34.6% sweet and 65.4% sour. DOE defines sweet as sulfur content no greater than 0.5% by weight and sour as greater than 0.5% but less than 2.0%; DOE's stated design ratio is about 40% sweet to 60% sour, based on likely US refinery needs, especially on the Gulf Coast.
claims.source: US Department of Energy (SPR Quick Facts)

claims.text: DOE reported the reserve at 284.9 million barrels as of September 11, split 96.8 million sweet and 188.1 million sour (Reuters). Against the August 20 DOE table, sweet drew about 5.0 million barrels and sour about 4.2 million over roughly three weeks, with sweet leaving slightly faster in absolute terms; the sweet share slipped to about 34.0%, drifting further from DOE's 40% design target. Note the September 11 split comes from secondary reporting of a DOE figure, not the published Quick Facts grade table.
claims.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine)

claims.text: The September 11 total sat about 32.5 million barrels above the 252.4-million-barrel minimum Congress mandates, so the exchange program has limited drawdown room left before hitting the statutory floor. DOE says it has secured cancellation of 140 million barrels of congressionally mandated sales scheduled for fiscal years 2024 through 2027, so there is no forced-sale overhang on the forward calendar.
claims.source: Reuters (via Permian Basin Oil and Gas Magazine); US Department of Energy (energy.gov)

claims.text: The next American Petroleum Institute (API) weekly crude oil stock change covers the week ending Friday, Nov 20, and is due on Tuesday, Nov 24 at 16:30 Eastern Time, with the official Energy Information Administration (EIA) Weekly Petroleum Status Report following on Wednesday, Nov 25 at 10:30 Eastern Time, a day before US Thanksgiving, Admiral Markets reported in a preview published on Nov 20, citing Trading Economics. The two previous API surveys showed large surprise builds of 9.0 million and 5.3 million barrels, and a consensus figure for the new week had yet to appear on Nov 20. The latest EIA report, for the week to Nov 13, had commercial crude rising by 3.38 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels, petrol stocks rising by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels, distillate stocks rising by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million barrels, and Cushing stocks falling by 1.2 million barrels to 26.1 million barrels, with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at 276.4 million barrels, down 3.1 million barrels on the week.

US commercial crude oil inventories rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended Nov 13, 2026, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its Weekly Petroleum Status Report published on Nov 18, a second consecutive weekly build that was larger than the 1 million barrel increase expected in a Wall Street Journal survey of analysts. Commercial stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) were about 3 percent below the five-year average for the time of year. Oil stored in the SPR fell by 3.2 million barrels to 276.4 million barrels, and oil stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the Nymex delivery hub, were down by 1.2 million barrels at 26.1 million barrels. The EIA estimated US crude oil production at 14 million barrels a day, up by 19,000 barrels a day from the previous week, with crude imports down 1.1 million barrels a day to 5.6 million barrels a day and exports up 1 million barrels a day to 4.5 million barrels a day. Refineries ran at 95.7 percent of capacity, up from 95.2 percent the previous week, although crude input to refineries fell by 129,000 barrels a day to 16.9 million barrels a day. Gasoline inventories increased by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels and distillate fuel stocks rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million barrels, 7 percent below the five-year average.
claims.source: Dow Jones Newswires (via Morningstar, citing EIA)

claims.text: US crude stocks rose by 5.28 million barrels in the week ended Nov 13, market sources said on Tuesday, Nov 17, citing American Petroleum Institute (API) data, Reuters reported on Nov 18. Gasoline stocks rose by 5.12 million barrels and distillate inventories rose by 351,000 barrels. The official Energy Information Administration (EIA) Weekly Petroleum Status Report for the same week is due on Wednesday, Nov 18, at 10:30 a.m. Eastern Time and had not been published at the time of the morning check, so the last official EIA figures remain those for the week ending Nov 6, when commercial crude stocks rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels.

A third 90-day extension of the Jones Act waiver for fuel shipments between US ports took effect at 12:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Monday, Nov 16, with no gap after the previous waiver expired late on Nov 15, Bloomberg reported via gCaptain. President Donald Trump extended the waiver on Nov 13, a White House official told Bloomberg and Reuters, without changing the breadth of the relief: foreign-flagged ships may keep carrying covered products, including gasoline, jet fuel, crude oil, naphtha, liquefied natural gas, soy oil and fertilizers, between US ports, and the case-by-case review introduced in August, under which the Maritime Administration is consulted on US-flagged vessel availability before the waiver is applied to an individual voyage, stays in place. An additional 90 million barrels of products, mostly refined fuels, have been shipped between US ports since the waiver was first issued in March, with gasoline, crude oil and renewable fuel the biggest beneficiaries, the official said; government data analysed by the Cato Institute counted 338 voyages on foreign vessels under the waivers since March. US Customs and Border Protection guidance puts the new loading deadline for covered cargo at Feb 14, 2027.

US crude oil inventories rose unexpectedly in the week ended Nov 6, ending a string of five straight weekly withdrawals, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its Weekly Petroleum Status Report published on Thursday, Nov 12, Dow Jones Newswires reported via Morningstar. Commercial crude oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels and were about 4 percent below the five-year average for the time of year; crude stocks had been expected to fall by 700,000 barrels in a Wall Street Journal survey. Oil stored in the SPR fell by 2.6 million barrels to 279.5 million barrels. Crude stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the Nymex delivery hub, rose by 106,000 barrels to 27.4 million barrels. Gasoline inventories rose by 1.8 million barrels to 210.8 million barrels and were 1 percent above the five-year average, while distillate fuel stocks rose by 4.1 million barrels to 103.3 million barrels and were 8 percent below the five-year average. Refinery capacity use rose to 95.2 percent from 94.5 percent, with crude input to refineries up by 322,000 barrels a day to 17 million barrels a day. The EIA estimated US crude oil production at 14 million barrels a day, up by 10,000 barrels a day from the previous week; crude imports rose by 325,000 barrels a day to 6.7 million barrels a day and exports fell by 220,000 barrels a day to 3.5 million barrels a day.
claims.source: Dow Jones Newswires (via Morningstar, citing EIA)

claims.text: The official US Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly petroleum report for the week ending Nov 6 is due on Thursday, Nov 12, delayed a day due to a US national holiday on Wednesday, Reuters reported on Nov 12. As of the morning check on Nov 12 the report had not yet been published, so the last official EIA figures remain those for the week ending Oct 30, when commercial crude stocks were 409.8 million barrels and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held 282.2 million barrels. Market sources citing American Petroleum Institute (API) data, reported separately on this page, put the US crude change for the week ending Nov 6 at a rise of 9 million barrels. Reuters noted the API build and the delayed EIA release in its Nov 12 market report, in which Brent futures were down $1.47 to $91.29 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures were down $1.24 to $85.29 by 0426 GMT.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated on Nov 10 that US crude oil inventories rose by 9.0 million barrels in the week ending Nov 6, after a fall of 5.267 million barrels in the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Gasoline inventories rose by just 4,000 barrels in the week, after rising by 1.427 million barrels the prior week, and distillate inventories rose by 1.5 million barrels, after a fall of 270,000 barrels the prior week, with distillate stocks already 13 percent below the five-year average heading into the period on the latest Energy Information Administration (EIA) data. Cushing inventories gained 182,000 barrels, after gaining 511,000 barrels the previous week. For the week ending Nov 6, 2.7 million barrels of crude oil left the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), bringing the reserve down to 279.5 million barrels, 434 million barrels below maximum capacity, API data reported by OilPrice.com said. Market sources cited by Reuters on Nov 11 put the same API crude change at a rise of 9 million barrels for the week ended Nov 6. The official EIA report for the week is due Nov 12.

The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its November Short-Term Energy Outlook, released Nov 10, that crude oil prices rose for a third consecutive month in October as falling global inventories, attacks on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, constrained shipping capacity and higher transport costs tightened supply, Fuels and Lubes reported. EIA expects the Brent crude oil spot price to remain near $100 a barrel for the remainder of 2026, before gradually falling to an average of $77 a barrel in the fourth quarter of 2027 as depleted global inventories rebuild. US commercial crude oil inventories fell to 410 million barrels at the end of October 2026, the lowest end-of-October level since 2014, and US crude oil production is forecast to reach a record 14.3 million barrels a day in 2027. EIA finalised its model inputs on Nov 5, so the forecast does not specifically account for market events after that day.

US crude oil inventories fell for a fifth consecutive week while distillate stocks fell to their lowest level in more than two decades, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said on Nov 4, Dow Jones Newswires reported via Morningstar. Commercial crude oil stocks excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell by 865,000 barrels to 409.8 million barrels in the week ended Oct 30 and were 4 percent below the five-year average for the time of year; crude stocks had been expected to slip by 200,000 barrels in a Wall Street Journal survey of analysts. Oil stored in the SPR fell by 399,000 barrels to 282.2 million barrels. Crude stocks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the New York Mercantile Exchange (Nymex) delivery hub, increased by 280,000 barrels to 27.3 million barrels. Gasoline inventories declined by 222,000 barrels to 209 million barrels and were 2 percent below the five-year average, while distillate fuel stocks fell by 3.6 million barrels to 99.3 million barrels, their lowest level since May 2003 and 13 percent below the five-year average, against an expected fall of 1 million barrels. Refinery capacity use rose to 94.5 percent from 92.8 percent the week before, with crude input to refineries up by 199,000 barrels a day to 16.7 million barrels a day. The EIA estimated US crude oil production at 14 million barrels a day, up by 11,000 barrels a day from the previous week; crude imports held steady at 6.4 million barrels a day, while exports fell by 1.2 million barrels a day to 3.7 million barrels a day.
claims.source: Dow Jones Newswires (via Morningstar, citing EIA)

claims.text: The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated on Nov 3 that US crude oil inventories fell by 5.267 million barrels in the week ending Oct 30, after a 2.031-million-barrel fall in the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Gasoline inventories rose by 1.427 million barrels, after rising by 2.39 million barrels the prior week, and distillate inventories fell by 270,000 barrels, after gaining 380,000 barrels the prior week, with distillate stocks already 10 percent below the five-year average heading into the period on the latest Energy Information Administration (EIA) data. Cushing inventories gained 511,000 barrels, after losing 453,000 barrels the previous week. Commercial crude inventories excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) have lost more than 64 million barrels over the last 29 weeks on API data. For the week ending Oct 30, 400,000 barrels of crude left the SPR, bringing the reserve down to 282.2 million barrels, 432 million barrels below maximum capacity, API data reported by OilPrice.com said. Market sources cited by Reuters on Nov 4 put the same API crude draw at 5.27 million barrels against a Reuters poll expectation for a rise of about 880,000 barrels, and put the distillate change at a fall of 1.19 million barrels, a different product figure from the OilPrice.com report of the API release; the official EIA report for the week is due Nov 4.

US crude and distillate inventories fell while gasoline stockpiles rose last week, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said on Oct 28, Reuters reported. Crude inventories fell by 1.9 million barrels to 410.6 million barrels in the week ended Oct 23, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a 15,000-barrel rise. Crude stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery hub fell by 624,000 barrels, and Gulf Coast inventories fell to their lowest level since December 2024. Gasoline stocks rose by 3.9 million barrels to 209.2 million barrels, against expectations for a 0.9-million-barrel draw, and distillate stockpiles fell by 1.5 million barrels to 102.8 million barrels, versus expectations for a 0.9-million-barrel drop. Refinery crude runs fell by 123,000 b/d and utilization fell 0.6 points to 92.8 percent. Net US crude imports fell by 796,000 b/d, while exports rose by 1.4 million b/d to 4.85 million b/d. Kpler lead oil analyst Matt Smith warned that EIA appeared to have significantly overestimated crude exports, with observed loadings about 1 million b/d lower than EIA reported.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated on Oct 27 that US crude oil inventories fell by 2.031 million barrels in the week ending October 23, after a 4.93-million-barrel fall in the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Gasoline inventories rose by 2.39 million barrels, after falling by 2 million barrels the prior week, and distillate inventories rose by 380,000 barrels, after a 2.6-million-barrel fall the prior week; distillate stocks were already 9 percent below the five-year average heading into this reporting period, on the latest EIA data. Cushing inventories fell by 453,000 barrels, after gaining 900,000 barrels the previous week. Commercial crude inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 58 million barrels over the last 28 weeks on API data. In the same report, 100,000 barrels of crude oil left the SPR in the week ending October 23, bringing the reserve down to 282.6 million barrels. The official EIA weekly report for the same week is due later on Oct 28.

US energy companies kept the total number of oil and gas rigs unchanged for a second consecutive week, Reuters reported on Oct 23. According to energy services firm Baker Hughes, the total rig count remained at 603 for the week ended Oct 23, an indicator of potential future production.

US crude and gasoline stocks fell last week, while distillate inventories rose, the US Energy Information Administration said on Oct 21, Reuters reported via TradingView. Crude inventories fell by 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels in the week ended Oct 16, compared with analysts expectations for an 820,000-barrel draw. Distillate fuel stocks increased by 1.7 million barrels to 104.3 million barrels, compared with expectations for a 1.3-million-barrel draw, and were 9 percent below the five-year average for the time of year, Dow Jones reported. Gasoline stocks fell by 3.0 million barrels. Crude stocks were about 3 percent below the five-year average.

The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated on Oct 20 that US crude oil inventories fell by 4.93 million barrels in the week ending Oct 16, after an 11.12-million-barrel fall the prior week, OilPrice.com reported. Gasoline inventories fell by 2 million barrels and distillate inventories fell by 2.6 million barrels, on top of a 1.5-million-barrel distillate fall the prior week, while Cushing inventories gained 900,000 barrels after gaining 1.823 million barrels the previous week. Commercial crude inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 56 million barrels over the last 27 weeks on API data. The official EIA weekly report for the same week is due later on Oct 21.

US crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Oct 19, ahead of the next EIA weekly report. The poll follows the Oct 15 EIA report of an 8.6-million-barrel crude draw to 415.6 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9.

EIA reported on Oct 15 that US commercial crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, against a Reuters poll expectation for a 288,000-barrel draw. Cushing stocks rose 1.9 million barrels, gasoline rose 3.5 million barrels to 208.3 million, distillate fell 2.5 million barrels to 102.6 million, and refinery utilization rose 0.8 points to 93.5 percent. The SPR was unchanged on the week at 283.0 million barrels.

API estimated US crude inventories fell 11.12 million barrels in the week ending Oct 9, after a 2.09-million-barrel fall the prior week, while no barrels left the SPR that week, leaving the reserve at 283 million barrels, still 431 million below maximum capacity. API also put distillate stocks down 1.5 million barrels and gasoline up 1.1 million barrels; official EIA figures were due later on Oct 15.

Gulf of Mexico shut-ins fell sharply by Oct 12 to about 604,503 b/d of oil, 29.63 percent of current daily production, and 531 million cubic feet a day of gas, down from a peak near 1.46 million b/d ahead of Hurricane Isaias landfall, according to the federal offshore regulator's operator reports. Only five production platforms still had personnel evacuated. Shell reported no damage at its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito and Appomattox assets and was redeploying personnel, BP was restarting production at Na Kika and Thunder Horse, and Chevron was restoring full production after curbing five facilities.

Gulf of Mexico oil shut-ins eased to 57.54 percent (about 1.17 million b/d) by Oct 11, down from 62.89 percent on Oct 8, with personnel evacuated from 32 platforms, down sharply from 121 at the storm's peak, as operators began returning crews to undamaged facilities.

Chevron reported it kept production running at four of its nine Gulf platforms through Hurricane Isaias while five were temporarily shut in, and said crew remobilization would continue through Sunday under standard storm recovery procedures at its onshore facilities.

Hurricane Isaias shut in about 1.46 million b/d of Gulf of Mexico oil production with 129 platforms evacuated as the Category 3 storm made landfall late Oct 9 near the Alabama-Florida line; WTI settled at $91.85 and Brent at $104.72 to start the weekend, with the market weighing storm damage against the Hormuz tanker-attack risk.

Germany's national oil stockpiling agency, EBV, issued a tender to sell diesel, heating oil and crude oil from strategic reserves, Reuters reported on Oct 23. This marks Germany's first such release since Group of Seven (G7) countries agreed in early October to draw on reserves, Reuters said. The tender was reported alongside the US Department of Energy's Oct 23 emergency SPR exchange for Phillips 66 Lake Charles as governments moved to address supply disruptions.

US President Donald Trump determined on Oct 22 that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense, a move that could open up US funding for fossil fuel projects, Reuters reported. In a presidential memo, Trump invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels. The memo said that without the actions, the US is not able to provide enough of those energy services in a timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations, and it did not mention specific projects that could be funded. Trump signed legislation last year that included $1 billion in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security, and Vice President JD Vance said the previous week that the administration would use the act to expand capacity at a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings.

The US Energy Department will make up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil available from its Northeast emergency reserve, OilMonster reported on Oct 21. The volume equals 31.5 percent of the roughly 1-million-barrel Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, the fuel will be offered through an exchange rather than a permanent sale, and companies receiving fuel must return the same volume plus additional premium barrels, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by Nov 13. New England residential heating oil averaged about $6.11 a gallon for the week of Oct 19 in the same report.

Two senior US Energy Department officials said on Oct 20 that Washington is working with refiners in the United States and abroad to increase fuel production as a diesel shortage pushes prices higher, Reuters reported via OilPrice.com. US retail diesel averaged about $6.32 a gallon, with the national average stuck above $6 at record highs. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said earlier this week, as quoted by Reuters: 'We are talking about reopening every refinery we can. There are dialogues there, and that's a tough challenge. I'm not saying all these are going to happen.' The administration has also invoked the Defense Production Act to motivate refiners to restart idle plants, an outcome OilPrice.com noted remains uncertain, and restarting idled refineries takes time and money, so it will not be a quick fix.

The IEA agreed on Oct 15 to accelerate the release of the remaining volumes from its March 2026 collective action, including over 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible, its governing board said after meeting on Thursday. Members had pledged more than 400 million barrels in March. Analysts noted the diesel volume looks like an acceleration of existing commitments rather than new barrels, below the 50 million barrels of diesel discussed earlier in a French proposal.

Details of the Oct 9 Trump-Putin diesel deal now total 4.8 million tons: 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 in November, 1 million after that, and up to 3 million more depending on Russian refinery condition; US diesel futures fell almost 5% to about $4.64 a gallon on the news while AAA's national average sat near a record $6.28.

OFAC General License 135, signed minutes before Trump's Oct 9 announcement, authorizes the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel through 12:01 a.m. EDT on April 7, 2027, while barring debits to US accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund and Finance Ministry.

Trump said he would soon issue a directive under the Defense Production Act aimed at expanding US refining capacity; three industry sources told Reuters it could take the form of a presidential memo, as record diesel prices collide with the Iran war's strain on supply.

President Trump announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, plus 500,000 tons in November, 1 million 'immediately thereafter' and 3 million more to follow; Treasury issued a general license sparing Russian diesel loaded as of Oct 9 from sanctions until April 2027, and diesel futures dipped on Friday. The IEA says Russian diesel output has fallen about 30% amid the refinery strikes.

Germany will release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, heating oil and crude from emergency reserves under the G7 plan, Economy Minister Katherina Reiche told Reuters on Friday, the largest European contribution so far; diesel and heating oil go first, with no product breakdown or timeline given.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Oct 8 that member countries still hold about 1.1 billion barrels of public emergency oil stocks, including over 200 million barrels of diesel, and stand ready to release more to the market if and when required.

In a televised national address on Oct 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu confirmed France will make 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves available to distributors at cost price over about three months (Nov 2026 to Jan 2027), projected to cut diesel prices at the pump by 12 to 18 euro cents per liter; he will sign a decree authorizing the operation.

Gasoline stocks rose 400,000 barrels (6% below the five-year average) while distillate stocks were essentially unchanged and sit 12% below the five-year average; four-week implied demand averaged 21.1 million b/d, up 0.7% year on year.

Supply to the market from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) peaked in the second quarter of 2026 at more than 1 million barrels per day, but those draws slowed to almost zero during October, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said in its Global Energy Security Data, reported on Nov 20. Other OECD countries also released strategic stocks as part of the International Energy Agency (IEA) collective action announced in March, with most of these volumes reaching the market in the second quarter. The EIA also pointed to the deliveries still to come: on Sep 29, the US Department of Energy announced an exchange that would offer 40 million barrels of crude oil from the US SPR for delivery to the market in November and December, and on Oct 15, the IEA announced it would deliver remaining committed strategic volumes to the market. The EIA expects more barrels from strategic stocks will hit the market, and in its November Short-Term Energy Outlook it forecast that Brent will average $99 a barrel in December and $86 a barrel next year, with global oil inventories beginning to increase given the recent increase in exports and production from the Middle East.

An analysis of Energy Information Administration (EIA) and Department of Energy figures published on Nov 12 set out the forecast path for the reserve from here. The EIA's November outlook has the Strategic Petroleum Reserve bottoming at 241.5 million barrels in the first half of 2027, then climbing to 293.1 million barrels in the third quarter and 344.7 million barrels by the end of that year, with its table putting the reserve at 248.5 million barrels at the end of 2026, below the 252.4 million barrel statutory floor set by the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. The barrels coming back are returns on the exchange program, not purchases: the DOE's Oct 29 statement put secured returns at more than 216 million barrels, including 44 million premium barrels, and the analysis noted that returns are spread from November 2026 into 2028, so the reserve rebuilds far more slowly than it drained.

An analysis of Department of Energy (DOE) award sheets and requests for proposals published on Nov 3 by Data 4 the People put the two latest exchange rounds at 40.55 million barrels in total: 23.8 million of the 40 million barrels offered in FY26 Release No. 4, and 16.75 million of the 17 million offered in FY27 Release No. 1. In the first round ExxonMobil took 16 million barrels, while in the second round trading companies took 91.9 percent: Trafigura 4.875 million barrels, Gunvor USA 4.6 million, Vitol 4.15 million and one other trading company 1.775 million, with Phillips 66 taking 1.35 million. Companies pick up the oil from November 2026 through January 2027. Returns for the first round run from April 2027 to December 2029, with minimum premium barrels of 7 to 17.5 percent; for the second round no oil is due back before October 2028, the last window ends in December 2029, and the minimum premium is 14 to 19.5 percent. DOE publishes only the minimum premium, not what each winner offered. If companies take all 40.55 million barrels and no borrowed oil comes back first, the reserve would hold about 242 million barrels, below the 250 to 300 million barrel range a Texas A&M petroleum engineering professor cited by CNBC called the practical operational floor, and the lowest level since early 1982; DOE has said at least 70 million barrels must stay in the reserve to manage its salt caverns safely, and analysts at Rapidan Energy describe a floor of about 170 million barrels.
claims.source: Data 4 the People (citing DOE award sheets)

claims.text: MBSB Research said in a sector thematic report dated Oct 30 that the planned replenishment of the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) could provide sustained support for crude prices over the next two to three years, Business Today reported on Oct 31. The research house said companies that borrowed crude from the emergency reserves are scheduled to begin returning barrels from Nov 1, 2026, estimated approximately 165 million barrels including repayment premiums are owed following the emergency releases earlier this year, and expected a realistic replenishment rate of between 150,000 and 200,000 barrels per day, potentially extending into late 2028 or mid-2029. It cautioned that SPR replenishment alone would not determine global prices, as the estimated daily purchases represent less than 0.2 percent of projected global oil production in 2027, and maintained Brent assumptions of $90 to $100 a barrel for 2026 and $80 to $90 for 2027. The Nov 1 start date is the research house's schedule, not a DOE announcement; DOE's Oct 29 awards statement said returns of more than 216 million barrels begin early next year.

OilPrice.com reported on Oct 16 that if companies take the full 17 million barrels in the new solicitation before any repayments arrive, SPR inventories would fall from about 283 million barrels to roughly 266 million, inside the 250 to 300 million barrel range generally considered the reserve's operational minimum zone. The June offer of the same final tranche drew agreement to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned.

The Oct 16 solicitation re-offers the remainder of the final SPR exchange tranche first offered in June, when companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels against premiums of up to 24 percent in extra barrels returned to the SPR, Reuters reported. Borrowers under an exchange return the crude plus premium barrels at a later date.

The DOE authorized an emergency SPR exchange of up to 4 million barrels (2 million each for ExxonMobil and BP America) to address supply disruptions from Hurricane Isaias, with the borrowed crude plus premium barrels to be returned in 2027. ExxonMobil's share accelerates deliveries of previously awarded SPR crude to keep Gulf Coast refineries running.

The bid window for DOE's sixth and final 40-million-barrel SPR exchange closed on Oct 6 at 11 a.m. CT, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026; the tranche completes the US portion of the 172-million-barrel pledge under the IEA-coordinated 400-million-barrel release, with borrowers returning the oil plus premium barrels.

The IEA said on Oct 3 that member countries have so far released about 325 million barrels of oil and oil products, more than 80% of the 400 million barrels pledged on March 11, the largest coordinated release in the agency's history. It remains unclear whether the G7's new 100-million-barrel release counts against the roughly 75 million barrels still outstanding under that pledge or comes on top of it.

The Department of Energy issued a request for proposal on Sep 29 for an exchange of up to 40 million barrels of SPR crude from the Big Hill and Bryan Mound sites, with deliveries under awarded exchanges scheduled for November and December 2026 and bids due by 11:00 a.m. Central Time on Oct 6; DOE says five prior solicitations awarded more than 133 million barrels and earlier exchanges returned an average 25 percent premium.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright clarified in a CNBC interview that Venezuela's heavy crude would not be placed directly into reserve salt caverns but could be swapped for light or medium US barrels, because much of Venezuela's oil is heavier and higher in sulfur than the crude traditionally held in the reserve. Analysts quoted in the piece cautioned that many of the Venezuelan fields would need years of development and reinvestment before producing meaningful volumes.

In June 2026 the Department of Energy (DOE) awarded contracts for a further approximately 53.3 million barrels of Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) exchange crude across all four sites (Bayou Choctaw, Bryan Mound, Big Hill, West Hackberry) under its late-April request for proposal, carrying an approximately 28 percent return premium (15.1 million barrels). DOE said about 35 million barrels had been delivered to market to that point and that earlier phases had awarded roughly 80 million barrels (45.2 plus 8.5 plus 26 million).

Other International Energy Agency (IEA) members' announced contributions to the 400-million-barrel coordinated release included 22.46 million barrels from South Korea and 13.5 million barrels from the United Kingdom, with Germany, Austria, and Japan also releasing stock (Japan's releases began in mid-March), per reporting in late July 2026. Aggregate member delivery progress beyond these pledges has not been published in a single authoritative ledger.

Federal law restricts non-emergency drawdowns once SPR inventories fall below 252.4 million barrels, and a 1981 GAO report advised against releases below 250 million except in a very severe emergency. With the reserve near 284 million barrels and another tranche now in motion, the legal floor is roughly 30 million barrels away.

The Energy Information Administration (EIA) Weekly Petroleum Status Report published on Nov 18 put crude oil in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) at 276.4 million barrels in the week ending Nov 13, 2026, down 3.2 million barrels from 279.5 million barrels in the week ending Nov 6, confirming the Department of Energy figure reported by Reuters on Nov 17 and keeping the reserve at its lowest level since August 1982. The reserve stood 134.6 million barrels below its level a year earlier, a fall of about 32.7 percent, and accounted for about 95.5 percent of the year-on-year decline in total US crude oil inventories: commercial crude excluding the SPR fell by 6.4 million barrels over the same year to 417.8 million barrels, leaving total crude including the SPR at 694.2 million barrels, down 140.9 million barrels from a year earlier.

Crude oil stocks in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell to 276.4 million barrels last week, the lowest level since August 1982, according to Department of Energy data reported by Reuters on Nov 17. The drawdown is part of the United States agreement to release 172 million barrels from the reserve, Reuters said. The figure sits below the last official Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly reading published on this page, 279.5 million barrels in the week ending Nov 6, 2026, and the next EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, for the week ending Nov 13, is due Nov 18, which will show whether the official weekly series records the same level.

The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held 279.5 million barrels of crude oil in the week ending Nov 6, 2026, down 2.6 million barrels, or 0.9 percent, from the prior week, Energy Factbook reported, citing Energy Information Administration (EIA) data updated Nov 12. The reserve was at 39.2 percent of its 714 million barrels of authorized storage capacity and at its lowest level since October 8, 1982, Energy Factbook said. The weekly series shows the reserve held 415.4 million barrels in the week ending Feb 27, 2026, a decline of 135.9 million barrels to the Nov 6 level.

The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held 282.2 million barrels of crude oil in the week ending Oct 30, 2026, down 0.4 million barrels from the prior week, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data reported by Energy Factbook on Nov 4. That is 39.5 percent of the reserve's 714-million-barrel authorised capacity and the reserve's lowest level since October 15, 1982. On EIA's weekly series the reserve has fallen 133.3 million barrels from 415.4 million barrels in the week ending Feb 27, 2026; the announced exchange volume and the measured decline are different figures, because exchanges, deliveries and returns do not map one-to-one onto weekly inventory changes.

The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) held 282.6 million barrels of crude oil in the week ending Oct 23, 2026, down 0.1 million barrels from the prior week, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data reported on Oct 28. That is 39.6 percent of the reserve's 714-million-barrel authorised capacity and the reserve's lowest level since October 15, 1982.

Stocks of crude oil in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell to 282.6 million barrels last week, the lowest level since October 1982, according to data from the Department of Energy, Reuters reported on Oct 26. The level is down from 282.7 million barrels for the week ending Oct 16, 2026. The recent drawdowns have been part of a US agreement to release 172 million barrels from the facility, Reuters said.

US Energy Information Administration data released on Oct 21 put the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at about 282.7 million barrels for the week ending Oct 16, 2026, down 0.3 million barrels on the week and its lowest level since October 1982, Global Energy Flow reported citing the EIA release. That is roughly 40 percent of the reserve's 714-million-barrel capacity and about 431 million barrels below maximum capacity. Including the SPR, total US crude stocks were about 699 million barrels.

In the same API report on Oct 20, 300,000 barrels of crude oil left the SPR in the week ending Oct 16, taking the SPR total down to 282.7 million barrels, OilPrice.com reported, still 431 million barrels below maximum capacity and inside the 250 to 300 million barrel range generally considered the reserve's operational minimum zone. That follows the DOE data that put the SPR at 283 million barrels as of Oct 9, the lowest since October 1982.

DOE data released on Oct 13 put the SPR at 283 million barrels as of Oct 9, unchanged from the prior week and still the lowest since October 1982, about 13 million barrels above the first reading in August 1982. Senator Martin Heinrich raised concerns about salt cavern integrity at current low levels, while the administration said the caverns can be managed safely.

The SPR fell another 784,000 barrels to 283.0 million barrels, taking cumulative withdrawals since late March to 132.5 million barrels; combined commercial and SPR crude stocks drew 3.97 million barrels in the week.

Stocks of crude oil in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 283 million barrels in the week ending Oct 2, the lowest level since October 1982, according to Department of Energy data reported by Reuters. The drawdowns are part of the U.S. agreement to release 172 million barrels under the IEA coordinated action, and the administration last week offered to loan energy companies a further 40 million barrels from the reserve.
